analysis.one_liner: Reauthorizes federal college aid with bigger grants and loans while letting for-profit colleges draw far more federal money.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after three hearings it stayed in the House education committee and died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would extend the main federal higher education law. It raises the authorization for Pell Grants to $5,800, allows year-round Pell Grants for full-time students, raises annual Stafford borrowing limits from $2,625 to $3,500, and cancels student loans for families of 9/11 victims. It also repeals the '90/10' rule that forces for-profit colleges to earn at least 10% of their revenue from non-federal sources, repeals limits on distance-education programs, lets for-profit schools compete for campus-based aid, and switches consolidation loans to a variable interest rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income and working students would get higher authorized Pell Grants, year-round grants for full-time students, larger Stafford loan limits, and lower origination fees. Families of 9/11 victims would have loans canceled. For-profit colleges and their owners would gain a new revenue stream: with the 90/10 rule gone, a school could fund itself almost entirely with federal student aid, and the repealed distance-education limits would open eligibility to online and correspondence-heavy schools.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the authorized maximum Pell Grant to $5,800 for academic years 2005-06 through 2010-11 and allows full-time bachelor's students two grants in a single year so they can attend year-round.
Raises first-year Stafford loan limits from $2,625 to $3,500 (and second-year limits from $3,500 to $4,500), directly increasing what students can borrow at subsidized terms.

Requires a new public 'college affordability index' comparing each school's tuition increases to inflation; schools that raise tuition far faster than inflation must file explanation and reduction plans, and schools that fail to comply can face public reports, accreditation notification, audits, and fines up to $25,000.

Creates a $1,000 'Pell Grants Plus' award for low-income students who completed a rigorous high-school curriculum, and increases authorized funding for TRIO ($835 million) and GEAR UP ($300 million) college-access programs serving low-income students.
Cancels federal student loan debt for spouses, surviving joint debtors, and parents of September 11 victims.
Reduces student loan origination fees and modifies need-analysis rules to change how aid eligibility is calculated.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of the proposed grant and program increases, and would bear the risk from for-profit colleges that can now bill nearly all of their revenue to federal student aid. Student borrowers who consolidated loans at the low fixed rates of 2004 would pay more under the bill's switch to variable consolidation rates. Traditional colleges face new reporting duties and potential fines under the affordability index.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the 90/10 rule would let for-profit colleges operate almost entirely on federal student aid dollars, removing the standard that historically limited taxpayer exposure to schools whose revenue depends on recruiting aid-eligible students; the CRS summary also notes the repeal of distance-education limits and for-profit access to campus-based aid.

The bill replaces the fixed interest rate on consolidation loans with a variable rate, which would raise repayment costs for borrowers who locked in the historically low fixed rates available at the time.

The $5,800 Pell maximum is an authorization of appropriations, not a guaranteed payment; like the other increases in the bill, it would still require Congress to actually appropriate the money each year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The immediate student benefits are real but modest: higher borrowing limits, lower origination fees, year-round Pell for full-time students, and a transparency tool that lets families compare which schools are raising tuition fastest. The Pell increase is aspirational on paper, since authorizations still depend on annual appropriations. The largest structural change runs the other way: repealing the 90/10 rule would have removed the main statutory brake on for-profit colleges drawing federal aid, and the variable-rate consolidation change would have cost borrowers at exactly the moment rates were historically low. A reader would be right to see this as a bill that offered students visible help while moving federal money toward the for-profit college sector.

outcome.mechanism: The House education committee held hearings on it in May, June, and July 2004 but never scheduled a committee vote or sent it to the House floor, and it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. John Boehner, chairman of the House Education and the Workforce Committee, introduced the bill on May 5, 2004, and it was referred to his own committee.
The committee held hearings on May 12 and July 13, 2004, and its Subcommittee on 21st Century Competitiveness held a hearing on June 22, 2004.

The bill was never marked up, never reported out of committee, and never received a floor vote in either chamber; the last action in the record is the July 13, 2004 hearing, and the record shows no Senate companion action.
The 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and all House bills not passed expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The for-profit college sector kept the existing 90/10 rule and distance-education limits that the bill would have repealed, so the protections against schools funded almost entirely by federal aid stayed in place. At the same time, students did not get the bill's proposed increases to loan limits, fees, or the Pell authorization, which is why Congress later passed a different, competing reauthorization in the next Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: For-profit colleges kept their limits; students gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors were Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so the record shows no evidence of how Democrats or the full chamber would have voted.

industries.note: The bill repeals the 90/10 rule requiring for-profit schools to earn at least 10% of revenue from non-federal sources, repeals distance-education limits on aid eligibility, and lets for-profit schools compete for campus-based aid. That would let these schools charge their tuition almost entirely to federal student aid, with the risk falling on student borrowers and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Student loan lenders and guaranty agencies
industries.note: The bill reauthorizes the Federal Family Education Loan program, extending guaranteed lending authority to 2015 and keeping private lenders in the federal loan pipeline rather than consolidating it into Direct Lending. Switching consolidation loans from fixed to variable rates favors lenders over borrowers who had locked in low fixed rates.

Schools gain from expanded Pell and loan limits that bring aid to their students, but face a new college affordability index, mandatory reporting and reduction plans if tuition outpaces inflation, and fines up to $25,000 for noncompliance.
